results.answer: Yes, you can have a template inserted automatically whenever you create a new file of a given type using the `auto-insert-alist` and `auto-insert` variables in Emacs. Specifically, you define entries in `auto-insert-alist` where the CAR is a mode name or a regexp matching the file name, and the CDR specifies what to insert (a file or skeleton) or a function to call. When a new file is created, Emacs checks `auto-insert-alist` and, if a match is found, inserts the specified template automatically. This behavior is controlled by the `auto-insert` variable, which determines whether to insert something when a new empty file is visited. [1]

can I have the matching bracket highlighted when my cursor is next to one
results.answer: Yes, you can have the matching bracket highlighted when your cursor is next to one using the option `show-paren-highlight-openparen`. This option, when set to a non-`nil` value (i.e., enabled), highlights an open paren when point is just before it. Since brackets are treated similarly to parentheses in this context, this setting will also apply to matching brackets when the cursor is next to them [1] (and also confirmed in [4] for similar behavior with whitespace at beginning/end of line). The default is non-`nil`, so it is enabled by default. Thus, highlighting occurs when the cursor is adjacent to a matching bracket. [1]

results.question: half of this email is misspelled, can emacs underline the bad words live while I write
results.answer: Yes, Emacs can underline misspelled words live while you write using Flyspell mode. To enable this, you can use the command `M-x flyspell-mode` to toggle Flyspell mode in the current buffer. If you want Flyspell to work in all text mode buffers, add `'flyspell-mode'` to `'text-mode-hook'` [1] or set up a hook for message buffers like `message-setup-hook` [5] with `(flyspell-mode 1)` [5] to enable it in message composition. Flyspell highlights misspelled words as you type or move across them, and it can be customized to check only words you typed or edited using `flyspell-check-changes` [1]

results.question: use-package lazy load bind key
results.answer: The correct way to achieve lazy loading of key bindings in `use-package` is by using the `:defer t` keyword to delay loading the package until needed, combined with `:bind` to define key bindings. However, the key binding itself is not lazy-loaded by default — it is applied when the package is loaded, and if the package is deferred, the binding will be applied after the package is loaded (i.e., when the user first uses it). This is achieved via `:defer t` and `:bind`, as described in extract [4] and [5] — the binding is set up during package loading, which is deferred by `:defer t`. Thus, the lazy load of key bindings is enabled by using `:defer t` with `:bind`. The binding is not applied until the package is actually loaded, which happens lazily when the user triggers the command or key sequence. This is consistent with the manual's explanation that `:defer t` postpones loading until needed [4] and that bindings are applied after the package loads [5]

results.question: how do I pop up a clickable outline of sections for my latex paper, I keep forgeting where things are
results.answer: Use `C-c C-o C-e` to show the text content of a section, and use `S-mouse-2` or `mouse-2` to toggle visibility of sections with the mouse. For a clickable outline, ensure Outline mode is active and use `C-c C-a` to show all headings, or `C-c C-q` to hide sublevels. The outline structure is based on asterisk levels, and you can use `TAB` or `S-TAB` to cycle visibility of sections or the whole buffer [2] and [3] respectively. For LaTeX export, ensure your Org file has proper heading structure and consider using `#+LATEX_CLASS` to customize the LaTeX output [1] if needed. results.question: how do I sotre a link to the place I'm at in my notes
results.answer: Use the `M-x org-store-link` command. This stores a link to the current headline, which can be inserted later using `M-x org-insert-link` or yanking [1] . For file links, if you're in a file, it will store the current location and encode the line's content as a search string for later retrieval [5] . To use it, ensure you are in an Org mode buffer and press `M-x org-store-link`. The link will be stored and can be inserted later. If you want to store a link to a specific location in a file, you can use a search option like `::255` or `::My Target` after the file path [5] . For example, `file:~/notes.org::255` will store a link to line 255 in the file. This is especially useful when you want to jump back to the same place later using `C-c C-o` [5]

results.question: make every use-package declerations install missing packages automatically
results.answer: Use the option `:ensure t` in every `use-package` declaration to automatically install missing packages. This ensures that if a package is not already present, it will be installed when the declaration is evaluated [1] . To make this behavior global for all packages, set the user option `use-package-always-ensure` to a non-nil value using `(setq use-package-always-ensure t)` [3] . However, for every declaration to install missing packages automatically, the explicit `:ensure t` is required in each case. [1]
